idiom_name: XState v5 typed machine (setup({ types }) + createMachine) driven by an actor
implementation_notes: TypeScript's version of the library route is the typed machine: setup({ types: { context, events } }) makes the event union and the context explicit, createMachine checks states, guards and actions against them, and state.matches('amount') narrows the state so the view switch is exhaustive - the events come from UI intents, the actions are the commands and the compiler rejects an event a state does not accept. What replaces the classic controller is the machine plus the actor that interprets it; when a statechart dependency is unwanted or the flow is small, a discriminated union of steps plus a typed transition table gives the same single decision point with no dependency (see the second variant), and a hand-written ApplicationController class is only worth keeping when the flow is dynamic enough that it must be assembled at runtime.
pitfalls: A machine's value is a string union, so state.value only narrows through state.matches; switching on a cast or on a plain string re-opens the exhaustiveness the types were meant to enforce.
Guards typed as async or reading mutable module state make legal transitions depend on hidden state; keep them synchronous and pure or model the work as an actor/invoked service.
Persisted snapshots carry a machine version: renaming a state without a migration leaves restored sessions in a state the new machine cannot match, so version the snapshot and fail loudly.

variants.name: typed transition table over a discriminated step union (zero dependencies)
variants.implementation_notes: The dependency-free form: a discriminated union of steps, a discriminated union of events, and a transition table typed as Record<Step['kind'], (step: Step, event: Event) => Step | undefined> so the compiler demands an entry per step and every illegal transition can return undefined (which the caller must handle). Exhaustiveness in the view switch is enforced with a never-returning assertNever; the controller is one pure reducer, trivially testable and serialisable. Prefer it over a library when the flow is a small typed graph and the transitions should be readable in one file; move to a statechart library when hierarchy, parallel states or visualisation start to matter.
pitfalls: Returning the current step for an illegal event hides bugs; return undefined and make the caller surface the error, or log the rejected (step, event) pair explicitly.
The table only enforces one entry per step kind - a missing event falls through to the fallback, so the (step, event) matrix still needs tests.
